title: comparison sorting algorithms and selection
concepts: A comparison sort learns ordering only by comparing elements; its general worst-case lower bound is Ω(n log n), while non-comparison methods rely on stronger key assumptions.
Stability preserves the original order of equal-key records; in-place status and auxiliary memory are independent tradeoffs from time complexity.
Merge sort recursively divides and merges ordered runs, giving predictable O(n log n) time and stable output at the cost of auxiliary storage in its common array form.
Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recurses on regions; pivot strategy and partition scheme affect balance, duplicate handling, and worst-case behavior.
Heap sort uses an implicit binary heap to achieve O(n log n) worst-case sorting with O(1) auxiliary array storage but is not stable.
Insertion sort is O(n²) in the worst case but performs well on small or nearly sorted ranges and is stable when equal elements are not shifted past each other.
Counting and radix sorts can beat the comparison lower bound when keys have suitable bounded or digit-based representations; they are outside the comparison algorithm inventory here.
Quickselect partitions to find an order statistic without fully sorting, with expected linear time under randomized pivots and quadratic worst case for poor pivots.
